The Fano plane and PG(3,2): strut = a XOR b

A strut is a point of the Fano plane; the three lines through it are the three axes of its octahedron. A picture shows a structure; it is not evidence that the structure means anything beyond its definition.

← Box-kite gallery

Left: Fano plane on e1…e7 (click a point s). Right: PG(3,2) on 1…15.
About this visual

What you are looking at. Left: the Fano plane on the seven imaginary octonion units e1…e7: seven points, seven lines, three points on a line, three lines through a point. A line is a triple {a, b, a XOR b}. Right: PG(3,2), the geometry on the fifteen indices 1…15 (the imaginary units of the sedenions): 15 points, 35 lines, 15 planes. The octonion Fano plane is one of those planes: the points 1…7.

How to read it. Left: click a point s. The three lines through it are coloured; each line {s, a, b} gives a pair of assessors (a, b) and (b, a), and that pair is one axis of the strut-s octahedron: the colours match the axes of the octahedron page. Right: click a point to see its seven lines; choose a line or a plane from the lists; the octonion plane is the plane marked 'O'.

What it shows. Why there are seven box-kites and why each has three axes: a strut is a point of the Fano plane and the three lines through it are the three reversal pairs. The assessor's two indices and its strut are a Fano line, a XOR b = s. Counts check by hand: each point lies on 7 lines, each line in 3 planes, each plane holds 7 points and 7 lines.

What it does not show. That PG(3,2) is a geometry the sedenion product uses for anything other than labelling; the engine's own overlap check (skeleton_overlap) is where that is measured. And it does not show e0, which is in neither plane.

Numbers to check. 15 points, 35 lines, 15 planes; points on a line 3; lines through a point 7; the 7 Fano lines of the octonions {1,2,3} {1,4,5} {1,6,7} {2,4,6} {2,5,7} {3,4,7} {3,5,6}.

running self-check…

Code and data. Everything shown is recomputed in the browser by bk.js (the Cayley–Dickson table by doubling, every product, the group by enumeration) and compared with the numbers the Python engine baked into bk_data.js.

  • ValaQuenta/modules/box_kite/maths.py: the Python engine these pages port and check against (Cayley–Dickson table, assessors, box-kites, associator, the labelled group)
  • ValaQuenta/wiki/box_kite.md: the engine's record page, including 'The group, enumerated'
  • Ainulindale/wiki/84_the_box_kite_debugger.md: the narrative of the box-kite as a debugger
  • ValaQuenta/tests/test_box_kite.py: the tests, including an independent recursive Cayley–Dickson product

Literature.

  • R. P. C. de Marrais, "Placeholder Substructures I: The Road from Zero-Divisors to the 84 Diagonal Sedenions" and "II: The Emergence of the Pentagonal Genes", arXiv:math/0207003 and arXiv:math/0207005.
  • K. Imaeda and M. Imaeda, "Sedenions: algebra and analysis", Applied Mathematics and Computation 115 (2000) 77–88.
  • R. E. Cawagas, "On the structure and zero divisors of the Cayley–Dickson sedenion algebra", Discussiones Mathematicae – General Algebra and Applications 24 (2004) 251–265.

  • J. H. Conway and D. A. Smith, On Quaternions and Octonions (A K Peters, 2003). The 1344 and the 168 in the labelled octonion group.
